# Lazy Dijkstra Distance Cache

Do not build the all-pairs distance matrix. The first time anything asks for `dist(a, ·)`, run **one**
Dijkstra from `a` and cache **every** `a→*` distance it produced along the way; every later query from
`a` is then O(1). Sources are populated on demand and never recomputed.

The insight is that Dijkstra is already single-source-all-destinations — stopping early at a single
target throws away work you have already done. Caching the whole row costs one array per source and
turns a repeated-query workload into an amortised one.

## Why it fits this workload exactly

In [[multi-depot-vehicle-routing]] the road graph is far larger than the instance. A 5000 m Wrocław
drive network is thousands of nodes; an instance uses 200 customers plus 5 depots. An all-pairs matrix
over the graph would be enormous and almost entirely unused, while an all-pairs matrix over just the
instance points would still need one Dijkstra per point up front — paid whether or not the search ever
visits that point.

Distances are also **directed** — one-way streets are respected, so `dist(a,b) ≠ dist(b,a)` in general
and the cache is genuinely per-source, not symmetric. The graph is truncated to its largest
**strongly**-connected component precisely so that a query can never fail to find a path.

## The behaviour it produces, documented rather than debugged

The visible consequence is a warm-up transient, and the spec calls it out so nobody reads it as a bug:

> "It is computed lazily: the first query from a source `a` runs one Dijkstra from `a` and caches every
> `a→*` distance; later queries from `a` are O(1). No upfront full matrix. Generation 0 is slow while
> the cache fills, then evaluation accelerates — expected behaviour, not a stall."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/ARCHITECTURE.md, 2026-07-10

That sentence is a small instance of [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]] — the surprising runtime
shape is written down beside the design that causes it, so the next reader does not spend an evening
profiling generation 0.

## The constraint it imposed later

The distance oracle is a concrete `Dist` type with a non-virtual `operator()`, and the GA takes it by
reference. That is fast — no vtable in the innermost evaluation loop — but it means an alternative
scorer cannot be substituted at runtime. When the LBBS variant needed a penalised distance function,
it could not be injected into the GA at all:

> "Cannot feed BannedDist into the GA (Dist has no virtual operator() and distance.hpp must not
> change)."
> — Optimization Methods/final_project/mdvrp/include/lbbs.hpp, 2026-07-10

So the two-phase LBBS design explores with real distances and applies the ban only in the final
decode. A performance decision in the distance layer became an architectural constraint two solvers
later — see [[soft-multiplicative-ban-penalty]] and [[workload-balance-vs-distance]].
